buddhist_core_teachings.title: Buddhist Core Teachings and Sutras
buddhist_core_teachings.description: Central Buddhist teachings organized by foundational concepts (Four Noble Truths, Eightfold Path, Three Marks) and major sutras (Heart, Lotus, Lankavatara)
buddhist_core_teachings.source: Pali Canon, Mahayana Sutras, Buddhist scholarship
buddhist_core_teachings.author: Siddhartha Gautama Buddha (recorded by sangha tradition)
buddhist_core_teachings.note: Core teachings extracted from multiple tradition branches (Theravada, Mahayana, Vajrayana) with emphasis on universal principles

teaching_01.title: The Four Noble Truths
teaching_01.content_summary: 1) Suffering exists (dukkha). 2) Suffering has a cause: craving/attachment (samudaya). 3) Suffering can end (nirodha). 4) The path to ending suffering is the Eightfold Path (magga)

application.practice: Contemplation of suffering, recognition of cause, cultivation of hope through path

parallels_in_other_systems.reason: Foundational recognition of suffering as starting point for transformation

interpretations.text: Birth, aging, sickness, death are suffering. Not getting what we want is suffering. Getting what we dislike is suffering.
Suffering arises from mind's resistance to what is; clinging and aversion create the felt quality of suffering
The very nature of conditioned existence contains suffering; even pleasures contain suffering because they are impermanent

each_truth_expanded.name: Dukkha (Suffering)
each_truth_expanded.content: All conditioned phenomena subject to change contain element of suffering

each_truth_expanded.name: Samudaya (Cause)
each_truth_expanded.content: Craving for sensual pleasures, craving for becoming, craving for non-becoming

each_truth_expanded.name: Nirodha (Cessation)
each_truth_expanded.content: Complete cessation of craving, which leads to Nirvana (extinction of suffering)

each_truth_expanded.name: Magga (Path)
each_truth_expanded.content: Eightfold Path: right view, intent, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration

applications: Recognize that suffering is not punishment but natural feature of unenlightened existence
Identify specific craving patterns in your life
Understand that liberation is possible and attainable
Commit to the path as practical remedy

teaching_02.title: The Eightfold Path
teaching_02.content_summary: The way to end suffering: Right View, Right Intention, Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, Right Concentration

metadata.structure: Three categories: Wisdom (Right View + Intention) · Ethical Conduct (Speech + Action + Livelihood) · Mental Discipline (Effort + Mindfulness + Concentration)

application.practice: Structured daily practice; often studied one aspect per month

parallels_in_other_systems.reason: Right action as virtue; ethical discipline as path

eight_aspects.meaning: Understanding the Four Noble Truths; seeing reality as it is, not through delusion
Cultivate thoughts of renunciation, good will, and harmlessness; abandon greed, ill-will, cruelty
Avoid lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, gossip; speak truthfully, helpfully, gently, meaningfully
Avoid killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, intoxication; act ethically, harmlessly
Avoid occupations involving harm (dealing weapons, poisons, intoxicants); earn living ethically
Cultivate wholesome qualities (mindfulness, concentration); abandon unwholesome ones (greed, hatred, delusion)
Maintain clear awareness of body, feelings, mind, and mental phenomena without judgment
Develop one-pointed mind through meditation; deepening states of absorption (jhanas)

deep_dive.three_fold_path: Wisdom (knowledge of reality) + Conduct (ethical living) + Mental development (meditation) together lead to liberation
applications: Practice one aspect per week or month for deep study
Examine which aspects are strongest, which need development
Recognize this as practical path, not ideal to aspire to but concrete steps to practice

teaching_03.title: Three Marks of Existence (Impermanence, Suffering, Non-Self)
teaching_03.content_summary: All phenomena are marked by: 1) Impermanence (anicca) — all conditioned things arise and pass; 2) Suffering/Unsatisfactoriness (dukkha) — arising from impermanence; 3) Non-Self (anatta) — no permanent, unchanging essence

metadata.structure: Interdependent principles; understanding one deepens the others

parallels_in_other_systems.reason: Change as fundamental; Wu Wei as flowing with impermanence

three_marks_detailed.description: Nothing remains static; all conditioned things are constantly arising, changing, passing
three_marks_detailed.realization: Accepting impermanence liberates from grasping; grief and disappointment arise from resistance to change

three_marks_detailed.description: Unsatisfactoriness arising from impermanence; even pleasant experiences end, causing suffering
three_marks_detailed.realization: Not that life is always painful, but that clinging to impermanent things causes suffering

three_marks_detailed.description: No permanent, unchanging self or soul; what we call 'self' is a process of five aggregates constantly changing
three_marks_detailed.realization: Identification with a permanent self is the root of delusion; liberation comes from seeing through this illusion

applications: Meditate on impermanence in nature (flowers blooming and fading, rivers flowing)
Notice impermanence in your own mind (thoughts arising and passing)
Investigate non-self through meditation on aggregates (form, sensation, perception, mental formations, consciousness)
Release clinging as you recognize impermanence and non-self directly

teaching_04.title: Dependent Origination (Pratityasamutpada)
teaching_04.content_summary: All phenomena arise in dependence on causes and conditions. The chain shows how suffering arises through ignorance → formations → consciousness → name-form → sense organs → contact → feeling → craving → attachment → becoming → birth → aging-death

metadata.structure: 12-link chain showing how ignorance perpetuates suffering cycle; understanding breaks the chain

parallels_in_other_systems.reason: Understanding causality; accepting what flows from causes
Tracing how unmanageability arose from powerlessness over addiction

teaching_05.title: Heart Sutra (Prajnaparamita Hridaya)
teaching_05.content_summary: Concise expression of emptiness (sunyata): 'Form is emptiness, emptiness is form.' All dharmas lack inherent, independent existence; this insight leads to liberation from fear

metadata.length: one page; among the shortest major Mahayana sutras, among the most profound

parallels_in_other_systems.reason: 'The Tao that can be named is not the eternal Tao' — ineffability of ultimate

deep_dive.key_passage: Shariputra, form is emptiness; emptiness is form. Form is not other than emptiness; emptiness is not other than form.
deep_dive.meaning: Emptiness is not nothingness but the lack of inherent, independent, unchanging essence
implications: Nothing exists in isolation; all phenomena are interdependent
The concept of a separate, permanent self is illusory
deep_dive.famous_mantra: Gate gate paragate parasamgate bodhi svaha — 'Gone, gone, gone beyond, gone altogether beyond, O what an awakening!'

teaching_06.title: Meditation (Bhavana): Samatha and Vipassana
teaching_06.content_summary: Two primary meditation practices: Samatha (calm/tranquility meditation) develops one-pointed concentration and mental stability; Vipassana (insight meditation) sees into impermanence and non-self, leading to wisdom and liberation

metadata.structure: Complementary practices; concentration provides stable mind for insight; insight illuminates reality

parallels_in_other_systems.reason: Prayer and meditation for conscious contact; spiritual discipline

samatha_meditation.benefits: Reduced mental chatter, calm, ability to concentrate

vipassana_meditation.focus: Observation of body sensations, feelings, mental states, dharmas (elements of reality)
vipassana_meditation.goal: Direct insight into impermanence, suffering, non-self
vipassana_meditation.benefits: Wisdom, understanding of how mind constructs reality, liberation

applications: Start with samatha to stabilize mind
Progress to vipassana to see into nature of experience
Alternate between practices based on mental state
Regular practice leads to transformation over time

freemasonry_degrees.title: Freemasonry Degrees and Principles
freemasonry_degrees.description: Initiatory degrees (Blue Lodge 1-3, Scottish Rite, York Rite) with symbolic teachings, architectural metaphors, and progression through levels of consciousness and spiritual development
freemasonry_degrees.author: Masonic tradition (attributed to King Solomon's Temple builders)
freemasonry_degrees.note: Syncretic system incorporating geometry, alchemy, Kabbalah, and esoteric Christianity

degree_01.title: Entered Apprentice (First Degree)
degree_01.content_summary: Initiation into brotherhood; symbolic death, rebirth, and illumination. Candidate goes from darkness to light. Key themes: rough stone being shaped, potential being recognized, obligation to brothers and self

application.practice: Ritual enactment; contemplation of symbols; study of geometry

parallels_in_other_systems.reason: Acknowledgment of powerlessness; beginning of journey

ritual_journey: Hoodwink (blindfold) — candidate begins in darkness, representing ignorance
Circumambulation — journey around lodge; orientation and testing
Obligation — candidate swears sacred oath to keep secrets and support brothers
Illumination — blindfold removed; sees light (Worshipful Master's candle); symbolic rebirth
Instruction — taught meaning of rough stone, square and compass, letter G

symbolism.rough_stone: The candidate's self; unworked potential waiting to be shaped
symbolism.light: Knowledge, truth, enlightenment contrasted with darkness of ignorance
symbolism.obligation: Binding commitment to principles and brotherhood; transformation from profane to initiate
symbolism.square_and_compass: Right angle and circle; material and spiritual; matter and spirit balanced

degree_02.title: Fellowcraft (Second Degree)
degree_02.content_summary: Journey of learning and labor. Stone is worked and shaped. Candidate ascends winding stairs, symbolizing path of knowledge. Introduced to five senses, seven liberal arts, and architectural principles

metadata.symbolic_meaning: Mental/intellectual development; active participation in growth

degree_03.title: Master Mason (Third Degree)
degree_03.content_summary: Completion of Blue Lodge. Symbolic death and resurrection; candidate becomes a Master Builder. Stone is finished and perfected. Central drama involves death and resurrection; candidate is figuratively slain and raised

metadata.symbolic_meaning: Spiritual transformation; perfection of the soul; completion of physical work

application.practice: Contemplation of resurrection symbolism; incorporation into builder-brotherhood

parallels_in_other_systems.reason: Death and resurrection; transformation and commission
Love and transcendence; mastery and service

central_drama: Death of Hiram Abiff, architect of Solomon's Temple (legendary narrative)
Candidate is figuratively slain during ritual
Resurrection of candidate; restoration to life and light
Revelation of secrets known only to Master Masons
Investiture as Master Mason; accepted into governing circle
symbolism: Hiram Abiff — Master Craftsman who knows the ultimate secrets (perhaps the Tetragrammaton/Name of God)
His death — loss of esoteric knowledge; fragmentation of the perfect stone
Resurrection — restoration of wholeness and knowledge through the craft's succession
Keystone — the perfect stone; the perfected individual; the divine spark within

implications.mastery: Not power over others but perfection of self; becoming a master builder of one's own destiny
implications.immortality: Not literal but spiritual; perpetuation of masonic principles beyond individual life
implications.responsibility: Master Masons carry the secrets forward; become teachers and guardians

cross_system_analysis.note: Preliminary; full comparative analysis follows assessment phase
foundational_themes: All four primary systems (AA, Hawkins, Jesus, Buddhist) begin with acknowledgment of suffering/limitation
All include sequential/hierarchical progression from ignorance/powerlessness to wisdom/mastery
All emphasize community/sangha/fellowship as essential to transformation
All distinguish between material/surface concerns and spiritual/ultimate reality
